summary:
Sverdlovsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks for transgender visitors are severe and have sharpened since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the international LGBT movement an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings address LGBT travellers directly. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. The propaganda law carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. The extremism designation of the International LGBT Movement carries 2-6 years for participating and 6-10 years for organising.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the International LGBT Movement since the 2023 designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison, while 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols; participants in the designated organisation face up to 12 years in prison.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. In Yekaterinburg, the oblast's largest city, a gay man was beaten and robbed on a fake date, and a local LGBTQ+ support group shut down after pressure, both reported on 21 October 2024.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume is rising as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget across the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as a second-class citizen after the designation.

The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Survey respondents in the Ural area were found to be more closeted toward relatives than the whole-study sample, indicating a stricter concealment norm around family in the oblast's wider region than in the study population overall.
localsOnly:
Residents of Sverdlovsk Oblast cannot obtain legal gender recognition or gender-affirming care, since both were prohibited nationally in 2023, and no anti-discrimination protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation. Administrative fines under the propaganda statute and imprisonment under the extremism designation apply to residents as well as visitors, and the closure of a Yekaterinburg LGBTQ+ support group under pressure, reported on 21 October 2024, removed one of the city's organised points of contact.

Coercion directed at transgender residents by their own families is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman, Ada, was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.

Protection on departure is available through the UK asylum route: the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement statistics specific to Sverdlovsk Oblast are sourced. The figures of at least 139 people impacted between 2022 and 2024 and 101 extremism convictions as of 30 June 2025 are national counts, and the inventory does not indicate how many arose in this oblast.

No source in the inventory documents violence against a transgender person in Sverdlovsk Oblast. The Yekaterinburg incident reported on 21 October 2024 concerns a gay man, and whether it was treated as an offence under the anti-LGBT legal regime rather than ordinary robbery is unresolved.

The survey finding that Ural-area respondents were more closeted toward relatives than the whole-study sample is reported through the UK Home Office note; the underlying study, its sample size and its fieldwork date are not identified in the inventory and remain unresolved.

Whether any LGBTQ+ venues, support groups or social spaces remain operating in Yekaterinburg after the support group closure is not sourced, and current local police practice toward transgender visitors in the city is likewise not documented.
